# Accelerators and ISA Extensions

## Concepts

Hardware/software partitioning starts from measurable needs. Hardware is useful for repeated work with high throughput or strict timing; software retains flexibility for policy and irregular control. Offloading adds communication, synchronization, and software integration costs.

A memory-mapped accelerator and a custom instruction create different contracts. The first exposes registers or queues; the second changes instruction execution and needs ISA semantics, toolchain support, and precise handling of exceptions and side effects.

## Implementation

Begin with a small streaming operation and a ready/valid interface. Define payload format, latency, ordering, backpressure, reset, and errors. Keep software-visible controls separate from the datapath.

Before choosing a custom instruction, write a reference function and specify operand/result widths and corner cases. For a memory-mapped implementation, define input/output registers or buffers, completion status, and interrupt behavior. Preserve privilege and isolation requirements at the hardware/software boundary.

## Hands-on Experiments

Compare a software baseline and hardware implementation on identical inputs. Measure transfer overhead as well as computation time. Report total cycles, workload size, resource use, and the configuration that produced the measurements.

Stress downstream stalls, reset during work, and malformed requests. Deliver the specification, reference model, RTL, automatic tests, and integration guide as a reusable IP package.
